findings.title: queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown require Python 3.13
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, but Queue.shutdown() and the ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs (3.11/3.12) this raises AttributeError at shutdown time (silently swallowed by the try/except, so workers are never told to stop and blocked worker threads never exit), and the `except queue.ShutDown` handlers would fail to even import-resolve at runtime. The graceful shutdown path is broken on supported Python versions; use a sentinel/Event-based approach instead.

findings.title: Failed messages are marked completed and their offsets committed, silently dropping them
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in a `finally` block, so when result_processor raises, the offset is still considered complete and the commit loop will commit past it. Combined with the fact that ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows all exceptions (logs only), any message that fails processing (e.g. DB error, bad subscription data) is permanently lost with no retry and no DLQ — the offset is committed so it will never be redelivered. The existing test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling even asserts this drop-on-failure behavior. There should be a retry/DLQ path or the offset should remain outstanding (blocking commit) on failure so the message is redelivered.

findings.title: Queues are unbounded — no backpressure despite docstring claim, risk of unbounded memory growth
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after enqueueing, so the arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as it can. If processing (DB-backed result handling) is slower than consumption, queues grow without limit, holding decoded messages and their Message objects in memory until OOM. The class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' guarantee is false as implemented. Either set maxsize and block/propagate backpressure in submit(), or bound total in-flight items.

findings.title: close() stops the commit loop before workers drain, losing final offset commits
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(), which is what drains the worker queues. Any messages processed after the last commit-loop iteration (up to the entire remaining queue contents at shutdown) will be processed but never committed. On restart/rebalance those messages are redelivered and reprocessed, which for non-idempotent result handling means duplicate side effects. The correct order is: stop accepting new work, drain queues, do a final get_committable_offsets/commit, then stop the commit thread.

findings.title: join() unconditionally calls close(), causing double shutdown and ignoring its timeout
findings.body: Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close() then join() on strategies. Here join() calls close() again: shutdown_event.set() and commit_thread.join() are harmless, but queue_pool.shutdown() runs a second time — each Queue.shutdown() (on 3.13) raises ValueError on already-shutdown queues (swallowed by the broad except, hiding errors), and worker.join() is called again. Additionally the `timeout` parameter of join() is accepted but never used, so a stuck worker blocks shutdown for the full 5s join regardless. join() should simply wait (using its timeout) for work to drain, not re-run shutdown.

findings.title: Worker thread death permanently stalls offset commits for its queue
findings.body: If an OrderedQueueWorker thread exits for any reason other than a clean shutdown — e.g. an exception raised by metrics.gauge or the sentry_sdk transaction wrapper inside the finally block, or a non-Exception BaseException from result_processor — the thread dies, but all offsets of items still sitting in its queue remain in OffsetTracker.outstanding forever. get_committable_offsets will never advance past the smallest such offset, so commits for that partition stop entirely, backpressure-free consumption continues enqueueing into a queue nobody reads, and memory grows until the process is killed. There is no liveness check or worker restart.

findings.title: Arroyo Commit callable invoked from a background thread concurrently with the consumer thread
findings.body: The commit loop thread calls the arroyo Commit function (which ends up calling consumer commit / interacting with consumer state) once per second, while the StreamProcessor's main thread concurrently polls the consumer and may itself commit or rebalance. Arroyo strategies normally call commit from the processing (main) thread; calling it from an unsynchronized background thread risks racing with the consumer during rebalances/shutdown and can produce errors or commits of stale offsets. This needs verification against arroyo's thread-safety contract, or the commit should be marshalled back to the strategy thread (e.g. via poll()).

findings.title: test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to salted string hashing
findings.body: The test asserts that 20 arbitrary group keys hashed with Python's builtin hash() (which is salted per process for str) land on exactly all 3 queues. With random salt it is possible (though unlikely) that fewer than 3 distinct indices are hit, making the test flaky across runs. Asserting `>= 2` or using fixed deterministic keys would be robust.

findings.title: A sentry_sdk transaction is started for every single message in every worker
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker wraps each individual result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction. At production uptime-result volumes this creates and discards a transaction object per message (20 queues × full throughput), adding significant per-message overhead and, if any transaction sampling is enabled, flooding Sentry with events. The batched-parallel mode wraps batches, not items; this should be a span or sampled/omitted entirely.
